strengths: Significance: Improving natural-language proof verification is useful. Figures 3 and 6 show encouraging error-detection and balanced-score gains across multiple model families, including on two human-annotated benchmarks.
Originality: Although pessimistic aggregation is acknowledged prior work, focused chunk verification and progressive subdivision with early rejection provide a useful practical extension.

Presentation and reproducibility: The workflows are easy to understand, Appendix A.2 provides complete prompts, and the paper specifies its principal hyperparameters, temperature, and evaluation metric. Reporting TPR and TNR separately makes the tradeoff visible.

The qualitative examples identify plausible benchmark defects, including the unjustified classification assumptions in Appendix A.3, Case 2. The paper also acknowledges weaker-model false alarms and the dependence of pruning efficiency on class composition. No material research-ethics concern is evident.
weaknesses: Soundness of the manual audit is a decisive concern. Appendix A.3, Case 6 declares the proof correct and dismisses the verifier's objections, but those objections identify genuine errors: union is not vector addition over F_2, and f(C)=C does not imply singleton neighborhoods or a permutation on C. For example, if every student loves every student, f(S)=S while every neighborhood is S. This invalidates a central step of the displayed proof and undermines confidence in the authors' adjudication of verifier errors.

The claim that most stronger-model false negatives reveal critical annotation errors is not supported by Table 1: only 9/20 GPT-5 cases and 5/13 GPT-5-mini cases are classified as critical. A majority appears only when minor issues are included, although Appendix A.2 explicitly instructs the verifier to accept minor, easily fixable issues. Reviewer qualifications, independent adjudication, and agreement statistics are unspecified. Auditing selected false negatives on one dataset also cannot establish near-human verification performance.

QiuZhen-Bench does not provide independent validation of the method. Its 300 evaluated solutions are labeled by GPT-5 using progressive@3/6, the same workflow being evaluated. Agreement can therefore reflect shared verification biases. No human validation of these correctness labels is reported; the extraction spot checks in Appendix A.1 address problem transcription instead. The collection of 1,054 questions should be distinguished from a validated proof-verification benchmark.

The experiments do not sufficiently separate improved discrimination from a more rejection-prone operating point. Rejecting whenever any review objects inherently trades TPR for TNR. Comparisons against majority voting and single-pass verification are informative, but intermediate voting thresholds, stricter single-pass prompts, and matched-TPR comparisons are missing. Requiring an explanation does not itself ensure sound objections, contrary to the argument in Section 2.

Efficiency and statistical claims exceed the reported evidence. Figure 1 provides useful price-weighted token comparisons for GPT-5-mini, but there are no confidence intervals or repeated-run estimates, the reasoning-budget settings behind individual points are insufficiently documented, and the claim of faster execution is unsupported by latency measurements. Progressive verification also requires sequential rounds. Comparisons with the cited agentic verification methods are absent.

Reproducibility remains incomplete: the selection procedure and identifiers for the 300-example IMO subset, class counts, exact model snapshots, output limits, and detailed chunking/stopping behavior are not adequately specified. Main numerical results are primarily graphical, and the supplied PDF's Code and Dataset labels have no usable link targets. Together with the annotation concerns, these omissions prevent reliable independent assessment of the strongest claims.

strengths: Significance: Improving natural-language proof verification is a useful problem. Progressive verification offers a simple, training-free workflow that combines whole-proof checks, focused chunk checks, and early stopping.

Empirical merits: Figures 1, 5, and 6 report improvements across multiple model families and two externally human-annotated benchmarks, alongside QiuZhen-Bench. Reporting both TPR and TNR makes the tradeoff between detecting errors and rejecting correct proofs visible.

Originality: Although pessimistic aggregation is acknowledged as prior work, the progressive, multiscale implementation is a potentially useful extension. Its simplicity does not diminish its practical value.

Presentation and reproducibility: The workflow diagrams and Appendix A.2 provide understandable descriptions and explicit prompts. Appendix A.3 also contains convincing examples of overlooked proof errors, particularly the unjustified classification assumptions in Case 2 and invalid integer-count bound in Case 3.
weaknesses: Soundness—benchmark dependence: QiuZhen’s 300 evaluation solutions are labeled by GPT-5 using progressive@3/6, the same procedure being evaluated (Section 3.1). Consequently, performance on this benchmark measures agreement with a teacher employing the proposed method, rather than independently established mathematical correctness. Human spot checks in Appendix A.1 concern problem extraction, not verification labels. Independent expert annotation is needed before this benchmark can substantiate the central effectiveness claims.

Soundness—the false-negative audit does not support the headline interpretation: Table 1 identifies critical errors in only 9/20 GPT-5 and 5/13 GPT-5-mini false negatives. A majority is obtained only by including minor issues, even though Appendix A.2 explicitly instructs verifiers to accept minor, easily fixable issues. Thus, the claims that most false negatives reflect annotation errors and that TPR degradation is largely illusory are not established under the paper’s own evaluation policy. The audit also covers only IMO-GradingBench, lacks a documented independent adjudication procedure, and cannot establish near-human-expert performance.

Soundness—the manual adjudication itself contains a concrete mathematical error: In Appendix A.3, Case 6, the authors declare the proof correct and dismiss the verifier’s objections. However, the proof incorrectly identifies set union with addition over F_2 and infers that f(C_f)=C_f makes the underlying relation a permutation. For example, if every student loves every student, C_f is the entire population, yet each singleton maps to the entire population; the claimed singleton-neighborhood structure is false. The verifier’s objections are valid. Case 1 also discusses coefficients A11–A22 that do not appear in the displayed proof. These problems undermine confidence in the audit used to reinterpret benchmark errors.

Evaluation and scaling: Rejecting whenever any review rejects necessarily increases error detection while potentially accumulating false rejections. The paper does not sufficiently distinguish improved discrimination from a changed decision threshold: comparisons against intermediate rejection thresholds, calibrated aggregation, or matched-TPR operating points are missing. The modest sampling budgets and absence of uncertainty estimates also do not establish sustained scalability. Requiring an explanation does not, by itself, ensure the explanation is sound, contrary to the argument in Section 2.

Efficiency and comparative evidence: Figure 1 provides useful price-weighted token comparisons with GPT-5-mini reasoning-effort settings, but these do not establish general superiority over long-chain reasoning. No measured latency supports the claim that parallel verification is faster, and progressive verification contains sequential stages. Comparisons with the cited agentic verification methods are absent, leaving the contribution’s advantage over relevant alternatives unclear.

Reproducibility and presentation: The manuscript omits exact numerical result tables, class counts, repeated-run variability, and the selection procedure for the 300 IMO-GradingBench examples. Model snapshots, token limits, and detailed subdivision/stopping behavior are insufficiently specified. The front-page Code and Dataset labels have no recoverable destinations in the supplied PDF. Dense plots without exact values make the magnitude and reliability of improvements difficult to assess.

Significance, limitations, and ethics: The observed gains support a promising specialized technique, but the near-human verification claim and proposed uses as training rewards require stronger independent validation. The discussion acknowledges distribution-dependent cost and weaker-model false rejections, but inadequately addresses correlated verification errors and method-generated benchmark labels. No material ethical violation is apparent; nevertheless, redistribution permissions and licensing for the collected examination problems are not documented. Overall, the useful idea and preliminary gains do not overcome the evidential and adjudication weaknesses.

strengths: Significance: Improving natural-language proof verification is a useful problem. The proposed workflows are simple, require no additional training, and could be readily incorporated into existing verification systems.

Empirical merits: Figures 1, 3, 5, and 6 show substantial improvements in error detection and balanced F1 across multiple model families, including on two human-annotated benchmarks. Reporting TPR alongside TNR makes the rejection tradeoff visible.

Originality: Although pessimistic aggregation is acknowledged as prior work, chunk-focused verification and progressive subdivision with early pruning constitute useful extensions. The cost-performance experiments provide practical evidence beyond a single accuracy comparison.

Presentation: The workflow diagrams and complete prompts in Appendix A.2 make the basic methods understandable. Several appendix examples, particularly Cases 2, 3, and 5, convincingly illustrate errors in proofs labeled correct.
weaknesses: Soundness—claims exceed the label-audit evidence. Section 3.4 claims that most false negatives from stronger models identify critical errors, but Table 1 reports critical errors in only 9/20 GPT-5 cases and 5/13 GPT-5-mini cases. A majority is obtained only by including minor issues, which the verification prompts explicitly instruct models to accept. The audit covers only IMO-GradingBench, describes no independent adjudication or annotator agreement, and cannot establish near-human-expert verification performance.

Soundness—the manual audit itself contains a demonstrable error. In Appendix A.3, Case 6, the authors declare the proof correct and dismiss the verifier's objections. However, union is not addition over F_2, and f(C_f)=C_f does not imply that individual neighborhoods form a permutation. For example, if every student loves every student, C_f is the entire set and every neighborhood is that entire set, contradicting the proof's singleton-neighborhood claim. This undermines confidence in the audit used to reinterpret measured errors.

Evaluation independence: The QiuZhen evaluation labels are produced by GPT-5 using the same progressive@3/6 method being evaluated. Agreement with these labels therefore does not independently establish correctness and may favor similar verification behavior. Human validation of extracted problem statements does not validate solution labels. An independently expert-labeled subset is needed before this benchmark can substantiate the advanced-mathematics claims.

Methodological controls: Rejecting whenever any review finds an error necessarily changes the acceptance threshold as sampling increases. Comparisons with majority voting and single-pass verification do not establish how much benefit comes from better error localization versus a stricter operating point. Budget-matched aggregation-threshold comparisons and TNR comparisons at matched TPR would clarify this. Figure 6 also shows substantial TPR losses for smaller models; requesting explanations does not itself ensure that their objections are sound.

Evaluation and reproducibility: Results use 300 selected IMO-GradingBench examples, 200 Hard2Verify examples, and 300 QiuZhen examples without confidence intervals or repeated-run variability. The manuscript does not adequately specify the IMO subset selection, class counts, per-call output limits, or exact numerical results underlying the plots. The token-price accounting is useful, but the separate claim of faster execution lacks wall-clock measurements and concurrency details.

Scope and limitations: The contribution is a promising empirical extension of an existing aggregation idea, but comparisons with the cited agentic verification approaches are absent. The paper acknowledges pruning costs and TPR degradation, yet repeatedly discounts the latter using insufficient audit evidence. No material ethical violation is apparent, although licensing and redistribution terms for the collected exam problems should be documented. Overall, the unresolved ground-truth and validation issues prevent acceptance despite the useful observed gains.

strengths: Significance: Improving informal proof verification at manageable inference cost is a useful problem. Progressive subdivision with rejection-based stopping is simple, model-agnostic, and potentially practical.

Empirical merits: The evaluation covers several model families and three verification datasets. Table 1 reports an improvement in balanced F1 from 0.768 to 0.833 on the full IMO-GradingBench, providing evidence beyond the selected 300-example subset.

Efficiency: Figure 4 presents performance–cost curves, and Appendix A.1 supplements token accounting with runtime and monetary costs. These measurements support a practical advantage over the evaluated fixed parallel-verification configurations.

Presentation and originality: The workflow diagrams and explicit verification prompts make the central idea understandable. Although repeated pessimistic checking is established, progressively refining the scope of verification offers a useful incremental contribution.

Limitations and ethics: The paper acknowledges false rejections, occasional degradation of correct solutions during refinement, and the lack of formal correctness guarantees. No material research-ethics concern is apparent.
weaknesses: Soundness—incorrect manual adjudication: Appendix A.4 Case 6 declares the proof correct and dismisses the verifier’s objections, but those objections are mathematically valid. Union is not vector addition over F_2, and f(C_f)=C_f does not imply singleton neighborhoods or a permutation. For example, if every student loves every student, f(S)=S while every neighborhood equals S. This invalidates a central step of the displayed proof and undermines confidence in the audit used to support the benchmark-reliability claims.

Soundness—overinterpretation of the annotation audit: Section 3.4 examines only selected false-negative cases, without specifying sampling, independent adjudication, or inter-rater agreement. Table 2 reports critical errors in 9/20 GPT-5 cases and 10/20 GPT-5-mini cases, which does not support the statement that most cases from these models contain critical errors. Minor issues are explicitly acceptable under Appendix A.3’s prompts and cannot automatically be counted as corrected benchmark labels. These results establish some annotation problems, not that the benchmarks are generally unreliable for frontier models or that GPT-5 labels are sufficiently trustworthy.

Reproducibility and label validity: Appendix A.2 explains extraction of 1,054 QiuZhen problems but omits the substantive proof-generation and annotation protocol: generating models and settings, annotation prompts and aggregation, evaluated proof counts, class balance, and independent label validation. Consequently, the substantial gains on this dataset cannot be interpreted confidently. The IMO subset-selection procedure and problem-solving prompts and iteration limits are also insufficiently specified.

Soundness—efficiency attribution is incomplete: Progressive verification combines focused checking with adaptive stopping, whereas the simple baseline uses fixed parallel reviews. Table 4’s GPT-5-mini pes@12 token consumption is approximately twelve times standard verification. A sequential or batched whole-proof baseline with equivalent early stopping is needed to isolate the benefit of subdivision from avoiding unnecessary calls. The reported comparisons demonstrate savings against the chosen baseline but do not establish that progressive segmentation is responsible for their magnitude.

Evaluation uncertainty and significance: Verification results lack confidence intervals or repeated-run variability despite stochastic sampling. Downstream evidence consists of six IMO problems without reported replication and twelve Apex problems with three trials. The IMO comparison yields 22 versus 17 points, but uncertainty and independent grading are not documented. Apex measures final-answer accuracy rather than proof validity. These experiments are suggestive, but insufficient to establish robust improvements in frontier proof solving.

Originality and scope: The main novelty is the progressive scheduling of existing repeated-checking and chunk-focused prompting ideas. This could justify acceptance with stronger evidence, but comparisons primarily cover direct verification, majority voting, and simple pessimistic checking rather than the broader verification workflows discussed in related work. Claims of stable scaling also require qualification: rejecting upon any negative verdict accumulates false rejections as checks increase, and the paper neither characterizes that tradeoff nor validates its claimed behavior on independently adjudicated data.

strengths: Significance: Efficient verification of informal mathematical proofs is a useful problem. Progressively checking smaller proof segments while retaining the full proof as context is a practical, training-free approach.

Empirical merits: Results span multiple model families and three verification datasets. Table 1 reports GPT-5-mini improving from 0.768 to 0.833 balanced F1 on the full IMO-GradingBench. Table 4 provides concrete token, runtime, and monetary measurements supporting practical efficiency gains.
Originality: Although repeated pessimistic verification is acknowledged as existing practice, combining hierarchical segmentation with early rejection provides a useful incremental contribution.

Presentation and limitations: The workflow diagrams and verification prompts make the basic method understandable. The paper acknowledges false rejections, small downstream datasets, and the absence of formal correctness guarantees. No material research-ethics concern is apparent.
weaknesses: Soundness—incorrect manual adjudication: Appendix A.4, Case 6 explicitly declares the proof correct and dismisses the verifier’s objections, although those objections identify genuine errors. Set union is not addition over F_2, and f(C_f)=C_f does not imply singleton neighborhoods or a permutation of the underlying students. For example, if every student loves every student, then C_f is the entire set and every neighborhood contains all 120 students. This directly contradicts the proof’s essential permutation claim. Soundness—overgeneralization from the annotation audit: Section 3.4 examines selected false-negative cases without specifying selection procedures, independent adjudicators, or agreement rates. Table 2 reports critical errors in 9/20 GPT-5 cases and 10/20 GPT-5-mini cases, which does not support the accompanying statement that most cases from these models reveal critical errors. Genuine benchmark mistakes are demonstrated elsewhere in the appendix, but this selective audit cannot establish corrected overall performance, broadly invalidate the benchmarks, or validate GPT-5 as a ground-truth annotator for advanced mathematics.

Experimental controls: The efficiency comparison does not clearly separate progressive segmentation from early stopping. Table 4 charges pes@12 approximately twelve times the standard verification cost, whereas progressive verification prunes rejected proofs. A sequential or batched whole-proof verifier with the same early-rejection policy is needed to isolate the contribution of segmentation. Comparisons against standard verification and majority voting alone also provide limited support for superiority over mainstream verification workflows.

Statistical support and downstream significance: The main verification curves lack uncertainty estimates or repeated-run analysis despite stochastic sampling. The IMO experiment reports only six problems without repeated trials or an independent grading protocol. Apex has twelve problems and three trials, with visibly variable outcomes; final-answer accuracy does not establish proof correctness. These experiments suggest benefits, but do not convincingly establish the claimed robust frontier-model improvements.

Reproducibility: Appendix A.2 explains extraction of 1,054 QiuZhen problems but does not adequately specify candidate-proof generation, the GPT-5 labeling procedure, label validation, or the number and class balance of evaluated proof-label pairs. The 300-example benchmark subset selection and downstream refinement prompts and iteration limits are also insufficiently documented. Providing verification prompts is helpful but does not resolve these gaps.

Calibration and presentation: Rejecting a proof after any negative judgment necessarily amplifies false rejections as well as error detection. The paper does not sufficiently characterize this tradeoff by proof length or checking depth, despite emphasizing lengthy proofs and continued scaling. Claims of consistently best performance and nearly illusory TPR loss exceed the evidence. Figures 4–5 are also densely packed, and plotted configurations are difficult to map to exact hyperparameters. Overall, the practical idea has merit, but unresolved evaluation and adjudication weaknesses prevent acceptance.

strengths: Significance: Efficient verification of informal mathematical proofs is an important problem. Progressive subdivision with early rejection is a practical, training-free approach that could improve verification-and-refinement workflows.

Empirical merits: The experiments cover multiple model families and three verification datasets, reporting both error detection and acceptance of correct proofs. On the full IMO-GradingBench, Table 1 improves GPT-5-mini’s balanced score from 0.768 to 0.833, with TNR increasing from 0.660 to 0.816.

Originality: Although repeated pessimistic verification is acknowledged prior practice, combining it with progressively finer contextual proof checking is a useful methodological extension. Comparing subdivision, repeated whole-proof checking, and reasoning effort provides informative empirical evidence.

Presentation and reproducibility: The workflow diagrams and Appendix A.3 prompts make the basic method understandable. Appendix A.1 reports runtime and monetary cost alongside tokens. The paper also acknowledges false rejections, imperfect labels, and variability in the small problem-solving datasets.
weaknesses: Soundness—an explicit error undermines the annotation audit: In Appendix A.4, Case 6, the authors declare the proof correct and dismiss Qwen’s objections. However, the objections are valid: set union is not addition over F₂, and f(C_f)=C_f does not imply singleton neighborhoods or a permutation of students. For example, if every student loves every student, C_f is the entire set and f(C_f)=C_f, but every neighborhood contains all 120 students. The proof’s central permutation argument therefore fails. This directly weakens confidence in the manual adjudication used to support the claim that apparent false negatives are largely benchmark errors.

Ground-truth claims exceed the audit evidence: Table 2 examines only selected false-negative cases, without specifying selection, independent adjudication, or reviewer agreement. Critical errors constitute 9/20 GPT-5 cases and 10/20 GPT-5-mini cases, which does not support the statement that most cases for these models reveal critical errors. Minor issues are particularly ambiguous because Appendix A.3 explicitly instructs verifiers to accept easily fixable errors. These observations warrant benchmark auditing, but do not establish that the benchmarks are broadly unreliable or validate GPT-5 as ground truth for a different mathematical domain.

Reproducibility: Appendix A.2 documents extraction of 1,054 QiuZhen problems but does not adequately describe generation of the evaluated candidate proofs, the GPT-5 labeling procedure, filtering, or class balance. The IMO subset selection and problem-solving iteration cap are also unspecified. The abstract’s 'Code is available at' has no visible URL. These omissions prevent reliable reconstruction of important experiments.

Efficiency attribution is incomplete: Progressive verification explicitly benefits from early stopping, while simple verification launches repeated whole-proof checks in parallel. A repeated whole-proof baseline with comparable sequential or batched early stopping is needed to distinguish the benefit of subdivision from scheduling and pruning. Table 4 shows substantial practical savings, but does not isolate their cause or establish superiority over stronger verification workflows discussed in related work.

Statistical support and significance: The main verification curves lack uncertainty estimates or repeated-run analysis despite stochastic sampling. The downstream evidence comprises six IMO problems with one reported result per setting and twelve Apex problems with three trials. The IMO improvement from 17 to 22 points is encouraging but insufficient to establish robust superiority; Apex answer accuracy also does not directly establish proof correctness.

Presentation and limitations: Claims of consistently highest performance, stable scaling, and frontier-model reliability are stronger than the evidence. Rejecting on any negative verdict also compounds false rejections as checking increases, so the operating range requires clearer analysis. Research-level proofs, training applications, and code verification remain prospective uses. No material ethical concern is apparent, but the unresolved audit and evaluation issues prevent acceptance despite the useful underlying idea.
